strengths: BiAlign presents a clear, relevant extension to knowledge distillation: matching teacher preferences over demonstration subsets alongside token-level output distributions. The method adds no inference cost.

Table 1 reports improvements across all five benchmarks, averaging 1.0 and 1.7 percentage points over Output-Align with the 13B and 70B teachers, respectively. Experiments with a larger student and the Phi family broaden the empirical support.

The matched-compute and additional-data controls are valuable. Training Output-Align on sampled subsets and reducing BiAlign’s training duration help distinguish the ranking objective’s contribution from additional computation or data exposure.

The presentation includes explicit objectives, pseudocode, and extensive ablations. Increased teacher–student agreement on preferred subsets for 500 held-out MMLU examples provides supporting evidence that preference alignment transfers beyond the training tasks.
weaknesses: The reliability of the modest improvements remains insufficiently established. Run counts, seed variation, confidence intervals, and paired significance tests are not reported. HumanEval improvements over Vanilla correspond to approximately one or two additional solved problems, while several ablation conclusions rest on differences of only 0.1–0.3 points. The consistent direction across settings is encouraging, but uncertainty should be quantified.

Evaluation reporting requires clarification. With 164 HumanEval problems and one greedy completion per problem, the reported FT and C-Pretrain scores of 14.2% and 13.2% cannot result from ordinary binary pass rates. Averaging across runs could explain this, but no averaging protocol is specified. Table 9 also lists GSM8K’s total dataset size without identifying the evaluated split. Exact splits, aggregation, prompts, and scoring procedures are needed.

Important reproduction details are missing despite the useful high-level description: the exact CrossFit task/sample selection, optimizer and scheduling settings, sequence-length handling, and QLoRA configuration. Loss reduction conventions are especially consequential because token-level KL and pair-level ranking losses have different scales. Equation 3 also needs a specified treatment of zero or near-zero score ranges. No implementation link is provided to resolve these ambiguities. Together with the uncertainty concerns, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The experiments support improved performance under the evaluated prompts more directly than improved ability to learn from demonstrations. There are no matched zero-shot versus few-shot comparisons on the same tasks or controlled demonstration perturbations that separate general model improvement from better context use. The preference-agreement analysis supports the intended optimization effect but does not establish that this effect causes the accuracy gains.

The claim of greater benefit on more complex reasoning tasks is overstated. In Table 2, absolute improvements are 1.9, 1.5, 1.1, and 2.0 points, which do not increase consistently with the proposed difficulty ordering. Larger relative gains partly reflect lower baseline accuracy, and the qualitative examples do not establish a general improvement in fine-grained reasoning.
